原文: Simple coats of layered cloth protect against glancing blows without restricting the wearer's movement, but it isn't much better than regular clothes.
Cured hide layered around the chest and back and padded with fur protects well against light cuts and impacts, but does restrict the wearer's movement slighty.
Laced rows of boiled leather platelets protect better than cloth and simple hide without restricting movement any more than hide armour.
A shirt of interlocking iron rings offers excellent protection against all weapons, but the coat is quite heavy and significantly restricts movement.
These primitive fur helmets are easy to make, but not as robust as more advanced designs.
Cured leather helmets offer decent protection from glancing blows.
Steel cap helmets require great expertise to produce, but can take a lot of punishment.
Some armourers have found that attaching a curtain of ring mail to steel helmets is an easy way to offer extra protection.
Adding goggles and a nose guard to an aventailed helmet not only yields a little more protection, but looks very impressive.
Simple utility axe intended for domestic work.
One step up from a tool axe, the bearded design makes it easier to use the axe in a fight.
A broader axe-head makes it easier to inflict damage on shields and flesh.
This design is the pinnacle of axes for combat use, facilitating all manner of tricks and unpleasantries.
Few smiths know how to forge steel in a crucible. Here the technique has yielded an axe of unparallelled durability.
A simple bow made from the wood of a willow tree. Useful for hunting animals, but not as good against humans.
Birch wood is strong and flexible, and yields an excellent hunting bow which is quite serviceable in combat.
A well built pine bow strung with horse-hair of matching quality, with a comfortable grip that ensures stability at full draw.
This fine bow is made from the wood of an elm tree. It is flexible and strong - a deadly weapon in the hands of a trained archer.
The wood of a yew is perfectly suited for a war-bow. This is a powerful and sturdy weapon, decorated with a fine grip and the highest quality bow string.
Simple utility axe-head stuck on the end of a long pole to extend its reach in a fight.
One step up from a utility axe, the bearded design makes it easier to use the axe in a fight.
A broader axe-head makes it easier to inflict damage on shields and flesh.
This design is the pinnacle of axes for combat use, facilitating all manner of tricks and unpleasantries.
Few smiths know how to forge steel in a crucible. Here the technique has yielded an axe of unparallelled durability.
Short one-edged blade of varying sharpness, attached to a wooden handle. Never leave home without one.
Long single-edged blade, just short enough to qualify as a knife, but long enough to do some serious damage.
The broader blade of this knife gives it more weight when slashing, and its point is not to be trifled with either.
An even heavier, longer, and thicker version of the already quite heavy, long, and thick seax.
This knife is very nearly a sword. Its lightly curved blade is strong enough to pry open armour like a clamshell.
Little more than a sharpened stick, the common spear is cheap and easy to use.
The tip of this one is cleverly shaped to pry through armour and offers limited slashing capabilities for the dextrous wielder.
Though pattern-welding a speartip might seem like overkill, the extra flexibility allows for more powerful and accurate thrusts.
Combining a clever design with masterful smithing technique, this spear is incredibly deadly in the right hands.
The quality of this spear elevates it from a common weapon to something resembling a religious relic.
Swords have little use other than for taking lives, but they are very good for that purpose.
By broadening the blade and sharpening both edges, a powerful and versatile weapon has been produced.
Pattern-welding a sword requires a high degree of mastery over the forge, but you can't argue with the results.
Despite the size of its blade, this sword is light and perfectly balanced. It's ornate hilt rests comfortably in any hand.
The state of the art of European smithing has produced a beautiful blade that feels like it could cut through a rock as easily as snow.
It may not be an elegant weapon, but a stone to the face at high speed will get the job done more often than not.
A stronger string and an improved release mechanism allows this sling to impart more power on each throw.
Wool spun tightly into a longer string, fitted with a better designed cradle for the projectile, makes this sling surprisingly powerful.
An unusual amount of ingenuity has gone into the creation of this sling. Its comfortable grip and carefully calibrated cradle makes it a joy to use.
This sling is so well made, so carefully designed, that comparing it to other weapons of its type is almost an insult.
Pine isn't the best wood for a shield, but it's abundant and it certainly beats blocking a blow with your arm.
Made from a fir cut down in its prime, this shield is tougher than its pine counterparts without adding too much weight.
Padding a pine shield with cured leather improves the structural integrity of the shield significantly and protects against slinters.
This durable leather-padded fir shield has been further improved by reinforcing the areas where its grip connects to the wood.
Shields like this hang behind the thrones of kings. With its sturdy build and beautifully painted cured leather, it might stop a charging bull.
